content.thinking:
This intervention leans on methodological transparency—describing instruments and rigor to signal competence and objectivity, which tends to produce a modest trust boost, mostly on the competence dimension. Similar process-transparency studies typically show small gains, around 1-3 points on trust scales, strongest on the primary outcome, though some may read the jargon as overly technocratic.

I'll set the numbers accordingly: trust_multidimensional around +2.2, trust_post around +1.8, distrust_post around -1.2, with smaller positive shifts across funding perceptions, institutional trust, belief, concern, and policy measures, and minimal effects on donation and newsletter behaviors given the dry, technical framing.

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: This arm is a 'process/competence' intervention: it details instruments, quantitative methods, and reproducibility, signaling that climate science is rigorous and data-driven rather than opinion-based. Such methodological-transparency texts reliably nudge the competence (and somewhat integrity/openness) dimensions of trust, but the text is dry, jargon-heavy, and says nothing about scientists' motives, benevolence, or policy — so I expect a small positive primary effect (~2 points on 0–100) rather than a large one. Downstream outcomes are attenuated by causal distance: single-item trust and belief are anchored on pre-treatment answers, distrust items respond weakly and asymmetrically, and policy/concern/behavior items are dominated by stable partisan priors, so I place these in the 0.3–1.2 point range. The text's emphasis on objectivity rather than engagement gives essentially no lift (possibly a wash) for scientists' policy involvement. Incentivized behaviors (real donation dollars, newsletter signup) almost never move detectably from a 2-minute read, so I forecast near-zero but slightly positive values.
